content_voiceover: This slide dives into why FLT3 inhibitors eventually stop working, resistance mechanisms, which is a favorite advanced topic for hematology fellows. The top half is a literature summary organized by drug. For midostaurin, N676K is a described resistance mutation. Crenolanib resistance involves F691L and an extracellular domain mutation K429E. Gilteritinib resistance is driven by F691L. On the right, other FLT3 inhibitors like quizartinib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and pexidartinib show overlapping resistance mutations at F691L and the D835 codon, D835 mutations recur again and again across different inhibitors, making it a hot spot for acquired resistance. The bottom panel is an oncoprint from real patient samples collected after gilteritinib progression. Look at the FLT3-ITD row in blue, five of forty-one patients, about twelve percent, actually lost their FLT3-ITD clone entirely at relapse, meaning a different, ITD-negative clone took over. The red boxes show newly acquired mutations, RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, NRAS, KRAS, BRAF, CBL, PTPN11, were the most common escape route, found in about thirty-seven percent of patients, more common than the FLT3 F691L gatekeeper mutation itself, which appeared in only about twelve percent. Overall, new mutations of any kind emerged in fifty-six percent of patients at progression, underscoring that resistance to FLT3 inhibitors is often driven by bypass pathway activation rather than the FLT3 gene itself.
keypoints: F691L is the most common shared FLT3 gatekeeper resistance mutation across inhibitors
D835 kinase domain mutations recur across quizartinib, sorafenib, sunitinib, pexidartinib
Twelve percent of patients lose the FLT3-ITD clone entirely at gilteritinib progression
RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, about thirty-seven percent, are the leading resistance route
New mutations emerge in fifty-six percent of patients at time of gilteritinib progression
keypoint_voiceover: F691L and D835 are the classic on-target gatekeeper mutations to know, but the bigger picture is that RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, not FLT3 itself, are the most frequent driver of resistance, found in over a third of patients progressing on gilteritinib.
